Fallout Shelter coming to Android next month!

Huzzah. I've been fortunate enough to play it right away when it came out on iOS, and it has been a lot of fun. For those of you wondering about the game experience:

In essence, Fallout Shelter is a tower builder game, themed to Fallout. There are a few notable differences though. The biggest difference is that when you build something, it is built- no waiting for construction, etc. You do have to earn caps, the in-game currency, but that is more of a progression mechanic, since there are a number of ways to earn caps in the game. Each dweller, the citizens of the vault, has the full SPECIAL set of stats, as well as level, HP, and happiness. There are different rooms you have to build in order to manage the three resources (power, water, and food) which you staff with your dwellers. They can also be given weapons to deal with radroach infestations and raiders, and apparel that gives the dweller a stat bonus. Weapons and apparel can be found by sending your dwellers out to the wasteland on exploration missions, which take time but is by far the most efficient way to find useful gear.

With most free mobile games, this one is monetized by in-app purchases. However, Fallout Shelter does this in one of the least intrusive ways I've ever seen. You can buy lunch boxes, each of which gives you four random 'cards' with one always being rare quality or better. These cards can be special vault dwellers, weapons and apparel, caps, or resources. It is always random, so you can't directly pay for power. You also don't need to buy lunch boxes. There is a rotating objective system that will occasionally offer a lunch box as a reward, and you can get one once a week by keeping your vault dwellers happy.

This game would not be a traditional Bethesda release without having bugs, and this game has it's share. I haven't seen anything game-breaking, but there have been some annoying issues. The biggest problem I've seen is that occasionally the health bars will not go away, and can clutter up the screen. I've also heard that the game runs poorly on lower end devices. I play on an iPad Air 2, and it seems to run fine. A bigger problem I have is that moving around dwellers requires you to drag them from place to place. Sometimes it can be difficult to pick the right dweller without scrolling the screen to just the right place, and occasionally you'll mess up your room assignments when you grab a dweller instead of scrolling. It's annoying, but short of adding a whole host of menus, I don't see a good way to fix it.

Overall, I really enjoy this game. No intrusive monetization, fun and interesting aesthetic, and a game that is appealing both for quick play and for those who like to micromanage. It is definitely worth your time to pick it up. Of course, this review is far from complete, so please let me know if you have any questions- I'll be happy to do what I can.
